title: Breaking Out of Age Silos
author: Other Feminisms
summary: This piece curates and reflects on reader responses to an earlier essay, 'A Large Family is a Polity,' which had shared Catherine Pakaluk's New York Times op-ed on siblings, focusing specifically on how belonging to a larger family gives children practice being responsible for people who are not their age peers. The author had asked readers where they saw the most age-mixing happening in their own communities, and reports that church and homeschool co-ops emerged as the two dominant answers, with one reader describing homeschool co-ops as 'some of the least age-segregated spaces' her family visits. Several reader voices are woven together to build a composite argument: William connects age-segregation to the historically unusual nuclear-family arrangement of living apart from extended family, arguing that a child in a multigenerational household would almost always have younger relatives around to develop parental instincts on, while Roxane describes how even a single sibling relationship has grown more valuable as her own children age into it. The piece closes on an underexplored angle raised by a reader named Mary, who notes that most 'big family' discourse seems to come from older siblings, and wonders aloud whether younger siblings in large families experience or discuss the dynamic differently, an open question the author explicitly does not resolve.
points: Identifies church and homeschool co-ops as the two dominant reader-reported sites of genuine age-mixing in community life, contrasting them with the near-total age-segregation of conventional schooling.

Surfaces reader William's argument that age-segregation is a historically unusual byproduct of nuclear-family living apart from extended relatives, since a child raised alongside cousins and nieces would almost always have younger relatives present to practice responsibility on.

Highlights reader Roxane's observation that the value of even a single sibling relationship compounds over time, becoming 'exponentially more helpful' as her own children grow old enough to form relationships with their aunt.

Closes on an unresolved question raised by reader Mary: that most public 'large family' discourse appears to be generated by older siblings, leaving open whether younger siblings in the same families experience or would describe the dynamic differently.

Builds its argument entirely through curated first-person reader testimony rather than original reporting, treating the comment section itself as a legitimate source of family-structure insight worth publishing and reflecting on.
quotes: What I liked most about her piece was her emphasis on how belonging to a larger family gave children a sense of belonging to/being responsible for siblings who weren't age peers.

Homeschool co ops are some of the least age-segregated spaces that we visit. This has been one of the best things about homeschooling. Church is another place where the kids can often interact with a variety of ages.

Most people historically don't live, as we do, away from extended family. If we lived in the same home or neighborhood as our cousins and uncles and aunts, the youngest child would almost always have nieces and nephews to bring out and train the instincts of parental responsibility in him.

I had only one sister, a year and a half older, and while she was my world in so many ways, I see how that has only become exponentially more helpful as my children grow and begin to have adult relationships with one another.

As the almost youngest of a large family, I'm really intrigued by how much of the big family discourse, at least in my experience, seems to come from older siblings. I don't know if that's just my experience or if younger siblings don't talk about it as much.
